### Grep Commands

As a reminder, _extended regular expressions_ as supported by  `grep -E` are:

| regular expression | matching string                                                                           |
|:-------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `c`                | non-operator character `c`                                                                |
| `\c`               | character `c` literally                                                                   |
| $r_1r_2$             | sequence of regular expressions $r_1$ and $r_1$                                                 |
| $r_1\midr_2$         | either $r_1$ or $r_2$                                                          |
| `r*`               | zero or more occurrences of `r`, where `r` is a regular expression for a single character |
| `r+`               | one or more occurrences of `r`, same as `rr*`                                |
| `r?`               | zero or one occurrence of `r`                                                |
| `(r)`              | same as `r`                        |
| `r{i}`         | `i` repetitions of `r`, e.g. `9{3}` = `999`                               |
| `r{i,j}`         | `i` to `j` repetitions of `r`, e.g. `9{1,3}` = `9│99│999`                               |
| `r{i,}`         | at least `i` repetitions of `r`, e.g. `9{3,}` = `9999*`                               |
| `r{,j}`         | at most `j` repetitions of `r`, e.g. `9{,3}` = `(9│99│999)?`                               |
| `[s]`              | character class, e.g. `[ab34] = a│b│3│4` and `[A-Za-z] = A│…│Z│a│…│z`                     |
| `[^s]`             | complemented character class, e.g. `[^0-9]` are all non-digit characters                  |
| `.`                | character class with all characters                                                       |
| `^`                | a fictitious character at the beginning of a line                                         |
| `$`                | a fictitious character at the end of a line                                               |
|`\<`                | a fictitious character at the beginning of a word |
| `\>`               | a fictitious character at the end of a word |

| `[^s]` | complemented character class, e.g. `[^0-9]` are all non-digit characters | | `.` | character class with all characters | | `^` | a fictitious character at the beginning of a line | | `$` | a fictitious character at the end of a line | |`\<` | a fictitious character at the beginning of a word | | `\>` | a fictitious character at the end of a word | | `\b` | a fictitious character at the edge of a word | | `\B` | a fictitious character that is not at the edge of a word | | `\w` | synonym for `[_[:alnum:]]` | | `\W` | same as `[^_[:alnum:]]` | | `[[:alnum:]]` | same as `[0-9A-Za-z]` | | `[[:alpha:]]` | same as `[A-Za-z]` | | `[[:cntrl:]]` | Control characters. In ASCII, these characters have octal codes 000 through 037, and 177 (DEL) | | `[[:digit:]]` | same as `[0123456789]` | | `[[:graph:]]` | `[:alnum:]` and `[:punct:]` | | `[[:lower:]]` | same as `[abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz]` | | `[[:print:]]` | `[:alnum:]`, `[:punct:]`, and ` ` (space) | | `[[:punct:]]` | punctuation characters, same as [!"#$%&'()*+,-./:;<=>?@[\]^`{\|}~] | | `[[:space:]]` | tab, newline, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return, and `' '` (space) | | `[[:upper:]]` | same as `[ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ]` | | `[[:xdigit:]]` | hexadecimal digits, same as `[0123456789ABCDEFabcdef]` |

---

Explain in one line each what the following grep commands do. The file `file.txt` does not exist, but you can create one.

```python
%%writefile file.txt

test asdf#asd

while
   while
test
    while
while with text
some more while text

$4.22

$.20

hello #world
foo#bar #42 trail#:
name = "Alice"; config = {debug: true}; msg = "end"
```

Overwriting file.txt

```python
!grep -E '^ *while\b' file.txt
```

while
   while
    while
while with text

Prints every line that begins with the word `while` (preceded by any amount of space); the trailing `\b` forces a word boundary after `while`, so identifiers like `whileloop` or `whilelies` are not matched.

```python
!grep -E '\B#\w+' file.txt
```

hello #world
foo#bar #42 trail#:

Prints every line containing a `#` that is NOT on a word boundary (so the `#` is preceded by a non-word character or start-of-line) followed by one or more word characters — in effect, hashtags that are not glued to the tail of a preceding word (so `#world` and ` #42` match, but the `#` inside `foo#bar` does not).

```python
!grep -E '\$(\.[0-9]+|[0-9]+\.[0-9]*)' file.txt
```

$4.22
$.20

Prints every line containing a literal `$` immediately followed by a decimal number of the form `.ddd` or `ddd.ddd` (i.e., monetary values such as `$.20` and `$4.22`); the match is not anchored to the start of the line.

```python
!grep -E '".*{.*}.*"' file.txt
```

name = "Alice"; config = {debug: true}; msg = "end"

Prints every line containing a double-quoted substring that has a `{...}` brace pair nested inside it (the greedy `.*` on both sides lets the outer quotes span across other quoted pieces on the same line).
